before.title: The open flat slab: an incomplete timelike geodesic, a Cauchy slice and global hyperbolicity
before.statement:
Let $A:=\mathbb R^4$ carry the flat structure $(\eta,N)$ of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with global inertial
chart $x=(x^0,z)=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, and write $e_0:=(1,0,0,0)\in A$. Put
$$M:=x^{-1}\bigl((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3\bigr)=\{p\in A:0<x^0(p)<1\},$$
an open subset of $A$, and let $g:=\eta|_M$ and $N:=\partial_0|_M$ be the
restrictions of the metric and of the time-orientation field; write $x$ also for
the restricted chart $x|_M:M\to(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Then:

**(a) The slab model.** $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) whose restricted chart
$x$ has the constant components
$g_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$; the Christoffel symbols of the
metric-selected connection vanish on $M$, the curvature of that connection
vanishes on $M$, and every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic
([[lem-gr-constant-component-chart-flatness]]). Every curve in $M$ is locally
absolutely continuous, future causal or future timelike for $(M,g)$ exactly
when it is so for $(A,\eta)$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]).

**(b) An incomplete timelike geodesic.** Fix $z_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and let
$$\gamma:(0,1)\to M,\qquad \gamma(s):=x^{-1}(s,z_0),$$
be the vertical line through $z_0$. Then $\gamma$ is a smooth future timelike
curve and a geodesic with affine parameter $s$ and unit tangent
$\gamma'(s)=\partial_0|_{\gamma(s)}$; its velocity satisfies
$\nabla_{\gamma'}\gamma'=0$. There is no geodesic
$\tilde\gamma:(a,b)\to M$ with $b>1$ (or $a<0$) whose restriction to $(0,1)$
equals $\gamma$: the parameter interval $(0,1)$ is the maximal domain of a
geodesic with these data. Moreover $\gamma$ does not converge to any point of
$M$ as $s\to1$ (it converges in $A$ to the boundary point $x^{-1}(1,z_0)$,
which does not lie in $M$); hence $\gamma$ is future-inextendible in the
sense of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d) and its affine
parameter is bounded above. The model is therefore timelike geodesically
**incomplete**: it carries an inextendible future-directed timelike geodesic
whose affine parameter domain is bounded.

**(c) A Cauchy slice.** The set
$\Sigma_{1/2}:=x^{-1}(\{1/2\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ is a spacelike embedded
hypersurface of $(M,g)$ and a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a) and (c)):
every inextendible causal curve of $(M,g)$ meets it in exactly one parameter
value. Hence $\Sigma_{1/2}$ is a Cauchy hypersurface.

**(d) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal and its causal
diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, $p,q\in M$, are compact; hence it is globally
hyperbolic in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c).

If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed. **(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$(U,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ in which every metric component
$g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ is a constant function on $U$. Then:

**(a)** Every Christoffel symbol of $\nabla$ in the chart vanishes
identically on $U$,
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,
$R=0$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that
is, for fixed constants $c^1,c^2,c^3$ the curve $s\mapsto
x^{-1}(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the
flat model of [[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its
global inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, written $x=(x^0,z)$ with
$z\in\mathbb R^3$ (clauses (a), (b) and (e) of that definition), and let
$\gamma:I\to M$ be a future causal curve in the class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then: **(a)** $x^0\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is strictly increasing.

**(b)** For every $c\in\mathbb R$ the level set
$\Sigma_c:=x^{-1}(\{c\})$ is a spacelike embedded hypersurface of $M$, and
every inextendible causal curve of $M$ meets $\Sigma_c$ in exactly one
parameter value; equivalently, $\Sigma_c$ is a Cauchy hypersurface in the
sense of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c). **(c)** For all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is
compact. **(d)** The model is strongly causal in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (b); hence it is
globally hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

**(b)** $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and

([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let causal
curves be those of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Convergent ends are extendible.** Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the general absolutely continuous endpoint argument in this clause. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a future
causal curve and suppose $b:=\sup I<\infty$ and $\gamma(t)\to x\in M$ as
$t\to\sup I$. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a future causal curve
$\tilde\gamma$ defined on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ whose restriction to $I$
is $\gamma$. Consequently a future-inextendible causal curve whose domain is
bounded above does not converge at its upper end, and the dual statement
holds at the past end.

**(b) Maximal geodesics have no limit.** Let $(p,v)\in TM$ with $v\ne0$ and
let $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$, as supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a). Then
$\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ does not converge to any point of $M$ as $t\to\sup I_{p,v}$
or as $t\to\inf I_{p,v}$ (where convergence at an infinite end means
convergence as $t\to+\infty$ or $t\to-\infty$ respectively).

**(c) Segments lie on inextendible causal curves.** Let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$
with $t_0<t_1$ be a future causal curve, or a past causal curve. Then there
is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ (same direction as
$\gamma$ in the case at hand) and a strictly increasing affine map
$\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to J$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma$. In particular, any
two distinct points $p,q\in M$ with $p\le q$ and $p\ne q$ lie on a common
inextendible causal curve, and likewise for the past relation.

**(d) Cauchy sets are acausal.** Every Cauchy set of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) is acausal in
the sense of clause (b) of that definition.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$(U,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ in which every metric component
$g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ is a constant function on $U$. Then:

**(a)** Every Christoffel symbol of $\nabla$ in the chart vanishes
identically on $U$,
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,
$R=0$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that
is, for fixed constants $c^1,c^2,c^3$ the curve $s\mapsto
x^{-1}(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

derivations.claim: (The slab model.) By [L2] the set $M$ is an open submanifold of $A$ with the restricted chart $x$, and the restricted fields $g=\eta|_M$ and $N=\partial_0|_M$ are smooth; the components of $g$ in the restricted chart are the constants $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $g(N,N)=\eta(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,g)$ and $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold. Applying [L3] to this chart gives the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols and the curvature of the metric-selected connection and the geodesic character of coordinate curves. Since $M$ is open in $A$ and $g$ restricts $\eta$, the notions of locally absolutely continuous curve, velocity and pointwise causal character agree for curves in $M$ whether read in $(M,g)$ or in $(A,\eta)$. This proves (a).

(Monotonicity and Lipschitz bounds.) Let $u:I\to M$ be a future causal curve of $(M,g)$. By (a) it is a future causal curve of $(A,\eta)$, so [L4] applies: $x^0\circ u$ is strictly increasing and $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))$ for $t<t'$ in $I$, and $x^0\circ u$ is locally absolutely continuous. This is the quantitative input used below.

(Cone characterization and convexity in the slab.) By [L1] and $g=\eta|_M$, the future cones at points of $M$ are those of the chart. Since $M$ is convex in the coordinates of $x$, the straight segment between $p,q\in M$ lies in $M$; if $q-p\in C^+$ (respectively $\overline{C^+}$) the straight path $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ is a future timelike (respectively causal) curve in $M$ from $p$ to $q$, so $q\in I^+_M(p)$ (respectively $q\in J^+_M(p)$). Conversely a future causal curve in $M$ is one in $A$, and [L5] gives $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ when $q\in J^+_M(p)$; for $q\in I^+_M(p)$ the strict cone membership is the same statement with $C^+$. Finally, [L6] gives $C^++\overline{C^+}\subseteq C^+$ and $\overline{C^+}+\overline{C^+}\subseteq\overline{C^+}$.

(The vertical geodesic, its maximal domain and inextendibility.) Let $\gamma(s):=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(0,1)$. Its coordinate path is $y(s)=(s,z_0)$, so $\dot y=(1,0,0,0)$ and $\ddot y=0$; by [L3] and [L8] it is a smooth geodesic with affine parameter $s$, and its tangent $\gamma'(s)=\partial_0$ satisfies $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1<0$, so $\gamma$ is a future timelike curve. Suppose a geodesic $\tilde\gamma:(a,b)\to M$ with $a<1/2<b$ restricts to $\gamma$ on $(0,1)$ and has $b>1$. In the chart, both coordinate paths satisfy the first-order geodesic system of [L8] with the same initial data at $s=1/2$, namely $(y,\dot y)=((1/2,z_0),(1,0,0,0))$, because the Christoffel symbols vanish; by uniqueness in [L8] the coordinate paths agree on $(a,b)$, so $\tilde\gamma(s)=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(1/2,b)$. But for $s\in(1,b)$ the point $(s,z_0)$ does not lie in $x(M)=(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, so $\tilde\gamma$ is not defined there — a contradiction. The same argument at the past end excludes $a<0$. Hence no geodesic with these data extends the parameter interval beyond $(0,1)$. If $\gamma(s)$ converged to a point $q\in M$ as $s\to1$, then continuity of the chart coordinate $x^0$ on $M$ would give $1=\lim_{s\to1}x^0(\gamma(s))=x^0(q)<1$, a contradiction; hence $\gamma$ is future-inextendible in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and its affine parameter is bounded above by $1$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ admits an inextendible future timelike geodesic with bounded affine domain: it is timelike geodesically incomplete. This proves (b).

(Range of an inextendible causal curve.) Let $u:I\to M$ be an inextendible causal curve (future-inextendible and past-inextendible). Suppose first that $u$ is future-inextendible, and put $T:=\sup\,(x^0\circ u)(I)\le1$, finite because $x^0<1$ on $M$. If $T<1$, then $x^0\circ u$ is increasing with limit $T$, and by the Lipschitz bound of step 2.1 the spatial curve $z\circ u$ is Cauchy as $t\to\sup I$: for $t,t'$ close to $\sup I$ one has $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le|x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))|\to0$. By [L9] it converges to some $z_\infty\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $u(t)\to q:=x^{-1}(T,z_\infty)$ as $t\to\sup I$, and $q\in M$ because $T<1$ and $T\ge0$. By [L7] the curve $u$ is then extendible past its upper end, contradicting future-inextendibility. Hence $T=1$. The past argument is the time reverse and gives $\inf\,(x^0\circ u)(I)=0$; so $x^0\circ u$ is a strictly increasing continuous function on the interval $I$ whose image has infimum $0$ and supremum $1$ and contains neither endpoint (all values lie in $(0,1)$). Therefore its image is exactly the interval $(0,1)$, and for every $c\in(0,1)$ there is exactly one $t\in I$ with $x^0(u(t))=c$: existence by surjectivity, uniqueness by strict monotonicity.

(Strong causality.) Let $p\in M$ and let $U\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<\min\bigl(x^0(p),\,1-x^0(p)\bigr)$ so small that the open set $V:=\{q\in M:p-\varepsilon e_0\ll_M q\ll_M p+\varepsilon e_0\}$ is contained in $U$; this is possible because $V$ shrinks to $\{p\}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (in the chart it is an open double cone around $p$ intersected with $M$). By the choice of $\varepsilon$, the points $p\pm\varepsilon e_0$ lie in $M$. Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a future causal curve with $\gamma(a),\gamma(b)\in V$ and let $a<t<b$. Since $\gamma|_{[a,t]}$ and $\gamma|_{[t,b]}$ are future causal curves, step 2.2 gives $\gamma(t)-\gamma(a)\in\overline{C^+}$ and $\gamma(b)-\gamma(t)\in\overline{C^+}$; since $\gamma(a)\in V$, step 2.2 gives $\gamma(a)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\in C^+$, and by [L6] $\gamma(t)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)=\bigl(\gamma(a)-(p-\varepsilon e_0)\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(t)-\gamma(a)\bigr)\in C^+$. Similarly $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(b)\in C^+$ and $(p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(t)=\bigl((p+\varepsilon e_0)-\gamma(b)\bigr)+\bigl(\gamma(b)-\gamma(t)\bigr)\in C^+$. By the convexity and cone characterization of step 2.2, $p-\varepsilon e_0\ll_M\gamma(t)\ll_M p+\varepsilon e_0$, that is $\gamma(t)\in V$. Hence no future causal curve leaves $V$ and later re-enters it, and $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal.

(Compactness of the causal diamonds.) Let $p,q\in M$. By the cone characterization of step 2.2, $$J^+_M(p)\cap J^-_M(q)=\{r\in M:r-p\in\overline{C^+},\ q-r\in\overline{C^+}\}.$$ The corresponding set $K:=\{r\in\mathbb R^4:r-p\in\overline{C^+},\ q-r\in\overline{C^+}\}$ in the chart is closed (the cone is closed) and bounded with $x^0(r)\in[x^0(p),x^0(q)]\subset(0,1)$; hence $K$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^4$ by [L9] and, being contained in the open box $x(M)$, it is a compact subset of $x(M)\cong M$. Therefore the diamond $x^{-1}(K)=J^+_M(p)\cap J^-_M(q)$ is compact in $M$.

(The Cauchy slice.) The set $\Sigma_{1/2}=x^{-1}(\{1/2\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ is the level set of the chart coordinate $x^0$ at a regular value, hence an embedded three-dimensional submanifold with a slice chart given by $x$; its tangent space is spanned by $\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ with $g(\partial_i,\partial_j)=\delta_{ij}>0$, so it is spacelike. By step 3.1 every inextendible causal curve of $(M,g)$ has $x^0$-range exactly $(0,1)$ and meets the level $x^0=1/2$ in exactly one parameter value; by clause (c) of [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] this says that $\Sigma_{1/2}$ is a Cauchy set, and with the first part a Cauchy hypersurface. This proves (c).

(Conclusion.) Part (a) is step 1.1, part (b) is step 2.3, part (c) is step 4.1. By steps 3.2 and 3.3 the model is strongly causal and all its causal diamonds are compact, which is global hyperbolicity in the sense of clause (c) of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]; this is (d). The same model is timelike geodesically incomplete by (b), so in this class global hyperbolicity does not imply geodesic completeness.

before.quote:
If
$y$ is inertial and $o\in M$, the tuple
$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,
\partial/\partial y^2|_o,\partial/\partial y^3|_o)$ is an **inertial frame**
at $o$; its vectors satisfy
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is
future-directed. **(f) Cone sets.** Let a vector $v\in T_pM$ have coordinates
$(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ in an inertial chart, write $v_s:=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Write
$$C^+:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0>|v_s|\}$$
and $\overline{C^+}:=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the coordinate cone
sets.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with

continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].

in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently

locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which

chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.

  $\gamma(b)=q$;

   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

**(a) The underlying manifold.** Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ be Euclidean four-space
as a set and real vector space ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), equipped
with its standard smooth structure, in which the identity map
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ is a global smooth chart
([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).
The coordinate vector fields $\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$,
$a=0,1,2,3$, are smooth vector fields on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), and at every
$p\in M$ the tuple
$(\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is a basis of
$T_pM$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

$2$-tensor field on $M$ whose components in the chart $x$ are the constant
functions $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]), that is
$$\eta=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2 .$$

$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: diagonal, with one negative and three positive
entries and no zero entry. Hence $\eta_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia
$(3,1,0)$, that is, a Lorentz form on $T_pM$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and $(M,\eta)$ is a smooth Lorentzian

([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The restriction of $\eta_p$ to
$\operatorname{span}(\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p)$ is positive
definite.

([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). The triple $(M,\eta,N)$ is

[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] applies, and a nonzero causal

**events** of the model. Since $M=\mathbb R^4$ is a vector space, for events

the **straight path** from $p$ to $q$ is the curve $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ on
$[0,1]$, whose chart representative has the constant velocity $q-p$. For
$v\in\mathbb R^4$ the **translation** is the map $\tau_v(p):=p+v$ of $M$.

$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $M$ and its first coordinate vector field
$\partial/\partial y^0$ is future-directed at every point. The chart $x$ of (a)

$(o;\partial/\partial y^0|_o,\partial/\partial y^1|_o,

$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ is

([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $k\in\mathbb N$ satisfy $0\le k\le m$,
and let $S\subseteq M$. One says that $S$ is an **embedded $k$-dimensional
submanifold** of $M$ when for every $p\in S$ there
is a smooth chart $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with $p\in U$
such that

$$\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}).$$

Such a chart is a **slice chart** for $S$ at $p$. The topology on $S$ is the
subspace topology inherited from $M$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

The next lemma proves that the restricted slice charts define a smooth
$k$-manifold structure on $S$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],

([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the
flat model of [[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its

**(c)** If $\gamma$ is future-inextendible then

model in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]
clause (e): its gradient is the vector field $\nabla u=-\partial_0$ on all of

everywhere.

Let $(M,\eta,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-flat-minkowski-model-and-inertial-charts]], with its global inertial
chart $x=(x^0,z)$, its cone sets $C^+,\overline{C^+}$ of clause (f) and its

**(b)** For every $c\in\mathbb R$ the level set

globally hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

=\{v\neq0:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

**(c)** If $v,w\in T_pM$ are future causal, then $v+w$ is future causal; if
one of $v,w$ is future timelike and the other is future causal, then $v+w$ is
future timelike. Equivalently
$C_p^++\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\subseteq C_p^+$ and

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$(U,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ in which every metric component
$g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ is a constant function on $U$. Then:

**(a)** Every Christoffel symbol of $\nabla$ in the chart vanishes
identically on $U$,
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=0$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b)** The curvature tensor of $\nabla$ vanishes identically on $U$,
$R=0$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]).

**(c)** Every coordinate curve of the chart is a geodesic of $\nabla$; that
is, for fixed constants $c^1,c^2,c^3$ the curve $s\mapsto
x^{-1}(s,c^1,c^2,c^3)$ is a geodesic in the affine parameter $s$
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

before.claim: (The slab model.) By [L2] the set $M$ is an open submanifold of $A$ with the restricted chart $x$, and the restricted fields $g=\eta|_M$ and $N=\partial_0|_M$ are smooth; the components of $g$ in the restricted chart are the constants $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $g(N,N)=\eta(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$, so $N$ is a time orientation of $(M,g)$ and $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold. Applying [L3] to this chart gives the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols and the curvature of the metric-selected connection and the geodesic character of coordinate curves. Since $M$ is open in $A$ and $g$ restricts $\eta$, the notions of locally absolutely continuous curve, velocity and pointwise causal character agree for curves in $M$ whether read in $(M,g)$ or in $(A,\eta)$. This proves (a).

(Monotonicity and Lipschitz bounds.) Let $u:I\to M$ be a future causal curve of $(M,g)$. By (a) it is a future causal curve of $(A,\eta)$, so [L4] applies: $x^0\circ u$ is strictly increasing and $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))$ for $t<t'$ in $I$, and $x^0\circ u$ is locally absolutely continuous. This is the quantitative input used below.

(Cone characterization and convexity in the slab.) By [L1] and $g=\eta|_M$, the future cones at points of $M$ are those of the chart. Since $M$ is convex in the coordinates of $x$, the straight segment between $p,q\in M$ lies in $M$; if $q-p\in C^+$ (respectively $\overline{C^+}$) the straight path $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$ is a future timelike (respectively causal) curve in $M$ from $p$ to $q$, so $q\in I^+_M(p)$ (respectively $q\in J^+_M(p)$). Conversely a future causal curve in $M$ is one in $A$, and [L5] gives $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ when $q\in J^+_M(p)$; for $q\in I^+_M(p)$ the strict cone membership is the same statement with $C^+$. Finally, [L6] gives $C^++\overline{C^+}\subseteq C^+$ and $\overline{C^+}+\overline{C^+}\subseteq\overline{C^+}$.

(The vertical geodesic, its maximal domain and inextendibility.) Let $\gamma(s):=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(0,1)$. Its coordinate path is $y(s)=(s,z_0)$, so $\dot y=(1,0,0,0)$ and $\ddot y=0$; by [L3] and [L8] it is a smooth geodesic with affine parameter $s$, and its tangent $\gamma'(s)=\partial_0$ satisfies $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1<0$, so $\gamma$ is a future timelike curve. Suppose a geodesic $\tilde\gamma:(a,b)\to M$ with $a<1/2<b$ restricts to $\gamma$ on $(0,1)$ and has $b>1$. In the chart, both coordinate paths satisfy the first-order geodesic system of [L8] with the same initial data at $s=1/2$, namely $(y,\dot y)=((1/2,z_0),(1,0,0,0))$, because the Christoffel symbols vanish; by uniqueness in [L8] the coordinate paths agree on $(a,b)$, so $\tilde\gamma(s)=x^{-1}(s,z_0)$ for $s\in(1/2,b)$. But for $s\in(1,b)$ the point $(s,z_0)$ does not lie in $x(M)=(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$, so $\tilde\gamma$ is not defined there — a contradiction. The same argument at the past end excludes $a<0$. Hence no geodesic with these data extends the parameter interval beyond $(0,1)$. If $\gamma(s)$ converged to a point $q\in M$ as $s\to1$, then continuity of the chart coordinate $x^0$ on $M$ would give $1=\lim_{s\to1}x^0(\gamma(s))=x^0(q)<1$, a contradiction; hence $\gamma$ is future-inextendible in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and its affine parameter is bounded above by $1$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ admits an inextendible future timelike geodesic with bounded affine domain: it is timelike geodesically incomplete. This proves (b).

(Range of an inextendible causal curve.) Let $u:I\to M$ be an inextendible causal curve (future-inextendible and past-inextendible). Suppose first that $u$ is future-inextendible, and put $T:=\sup\,(x^0\circ u)(I)\le1$, finite because $x^0<1$ on $M$. If $T<1$, then $x^0\circ u$ is increasing with limit $T$, and by the Lipschitz bound of step 2.1 the spatial curve $z\circ u$ is Cauchy as $t\to\sup I$: for $t,t'$ close to $\sup I$ one has $|z(u(t'))-z(u(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le|x^0(u(t'))-x^0(u(t))|\to0$. By [L9] it converges to some $z_\infty\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $u(t)\to q:=x^{-1}(T,z_\infty)$ as $t\to\sup I$, and $q\in M$ because $T<1$ and $T\ge0$. By [L7] the curve $u$ is then extendible past its upper end, contradicting future-inextendibility. Hence $T=1$. The past argument is the time reverse and gives $\inf\,(x^0\circ u)(I)=0$; so $x^0\circ u$ is a strictly increasing continuous function on the interval $I$ whose image has infimum $0$ and supremum $1$ and contains neither endpoint (all values lie in $(0,1)$). Therefore its image is exactly the interval $(0,1)$, and for every $c\in(0,1)$ there is exactly one $t\in I$ with $x^0(u(t))=c$: existence by surjectivity, uniqueness by strict monotonicity.

(Strong causality.) Let $p\in M$ and let $U\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and

where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction

about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
